# Bibliographic coupling and co-citation

::: {.learning-objectives}
**Learning objectives**

- Distinguish bibliographic coupling from co-citation.
- Use each technique for the question it actually answers.
- Interpret clusters using representative documents and references.
:::

## Core distinction

| Feature | Bibliographic coupling | Co-citation |
|---|---|---|
| Link | Two documents share references | Two earlier works are cited together |
| Main unit | Publications in the corpus | References cited by the corpus |
| Best use | Current research fronts | Intellectual foundations |
| Time behaviour | Reference lists are fixed at publication | Co-citation strength can grow with new papers |
| Classic origin | @kessler1963 | @small1973 |

## Prerequisite

Both analyses require a complete, consistently parsed cited-reference field `CR`. If cited references are missing from a large share of records, the resulting network is selective.

```{r}
#| label: citation-network-load

source(here::here("R", "00_setup.R"))
M <- as.data.frame(load_demo_data())

M |>
  summarise(
    field = "CR",
    available = sum(!is.na(CR) & nzchar(trimws(as.character(CR)))),
    total = n(),
    percent_available = round(100 * available / total, 1)
  )
```

## Document bibliographic coupling

```{r}
#| label: coupling-run

coupling_matrix <- bibliometrix::biblioNetwork(
  M,
  analysis = "coupling",
  network = "references",
  sep = ";"
)

coupling_plot <- bibliometrix::networkPlot(
  coupling_matrix,
  normalize = "association",
  weighted = TRUE,
  n = min(40, nrow(coupling_matrix)),
  Title = "Document bibliographic coupling",
  type = "fruchterman",
  size = 5,
  size.cex = TRUE,
  remove.multiple = FALSE,
  labelsize = 0.7,
  community.repulsion = 0,
  seed = 20261126
)

coupling_statistics <- bibliometrix::networkStat(coupling_matrix)
```

Interpret a coupling cluster by reading the titles, abstracts, publication years, shared references, and clinical indications of its leading documents. Do not name a cluster from one highly cited paper.

## Reference co-citation

```{r}
#| label: cocitation-run

cocitation_matrix <- bibliometrix::biblioNetwork(
  M,
  analysis = "co-citation",
  network = "references",
  sep = ";"
)

cocitation_plot <- bibliometrix::networkPlot(
  cocitation_matrix,
  normalize = "association",
  weighted = TRUE,
  n = min(40, nrow(cocitation_matrix)),
  Title = "Reference co-citation network",
  type = "fruchterman",
  size = 5,
  size.cex = TRUE,
  remove.multiple = FALSE,
  labelsize = 0.7,
  community.repulsion = 0,
  seed = 20261126
)

cocitation_statistics <- bibliometrix::networkStat(cocitation_matrix)
```

Co-citation clusters may represent foundational trials, measurement traditions, clinical guidelines, or methodological schools. A frequently co-cited paper is influential within the reference structure; it is not automatically high quality.

## Network statistics

```{r}
#| label: citation-network-statistics

summary(coupling_statistics, k = 10)
summary(cocitation_statistics, k = 10)
```

Useful statistics include network size, density, transitivity, centrality, and component structure. Their interpretation depends on the network definition and threshold.

## Validation questions

- Are the cited references consistently formatted?
- Do clusters remain after normalisation?
- Are review articles disproportionately central?
- Are recent documents disadvantaged in co-citation analysis?
- Do high-degree references correspond to the clinical history of FCM?
- Are the same research fronts visible in thematic mapping and coupling?

## Exercise

Compare the largest coupling cluster with the most central thematic-map cluster. Explain why the two structures need not be identical.
